story_text.value:
A few years ago when Stable Diffusion was released, I happened to be reading Homer's Iliad and came across a section where Achilles' shield is described in great detail. I fed the passage into Stable Diffusion, wondering how well it would do in creating an illustration of the shield. Of course it was terrible, but a year later DALL-E 3 seemed to do a pretty good job, as long as you didn't look too hard at the details. By then I had been reading Gibbon's Decline and Fall of the Roman Empire (yes I had been on a classics binge), and created a Python app that let me feed random paragraphs into DALL-E 3. The results were often grand collages that seemed to look like a combination of Renaissance art and graffiti.

After playing around with this idea for a bit, I realized it would be pretty cool to have a dedicated app that could download public-domain books and illustrate them with DALL-E 3. I have been working on this idea for a few years, at first copying code back and forth from Xcode to the ChatGPT prompt, and then later using Claude Code. I didn't know anything about developing for the iPhone, and had to tackle a broad range of issues, everything from setting up a serverless backend to writing code in Swift to releasing an app on the App Store. Technical issues as mundane as how to parse an EPUB correctly or how to create an engaging UI/UX were surprisingly complex.

Now this work has finally culminated in an app I call ParaGraFX: a free-to-download EPUB book reader with built-in text-to-image generation. This app is designed to make public-domain books easy to download and illustrate, with download tools for Project Gutenberg, Standard Ebooks, and The Internet Archive, and illustrations powered by fal.ai and OpenAI.

To get started just download the app and open one of the bundled books to start reading. At the bottom of the screen is a button labeled 'Illustrate', which can create an illustration based on selected text or the text on screen. Are you reading the section in Alice in Wonderland about the Mad Hatter's tea party? Just hit 'Illustrate' and you will be served with a custom illustration in one of three dozen styles — from Romantic oil painting, Japanese woodblock print and Art Deco poster to Byzantine mosaic, a cross-stitch sampler, 16-bit pixel art, or 1980s teletext block graphics. You can modify the generated illustration by either editing the original prompt, or providing custom instructions, such as adding the Queen of Hearts in the background.

This app is free to download and use for reading EPUBs, but since images cost money to generate, they are paid for with credits. The first 3 credits are free, and additional credits are available for purchase starting at $1.99 for 10 credits. There are 4 tiers of image quality that cost different numbers of credits, with the Fast tier costing 1 credit per image, and 5 credits for the Best tier, which uses OpenAI's top image model. (The free 3 credits are restricted to the Fast tier.)

I invite you to try it out and give me feedback in the comments. Whether you want to use it as a serious reader, or want to surf from book to book just to create illustrations, ParaGraFX grew out of the simple pleasure of illustrating the classics.

title.value: Show HN: ParaGraFX – An iOS app for reading and illustrating ePub books

story_text.value:
Kavela’s closed beta is out. AI agent automations that do not fail silently.

There are now 216 unique users in our closed-beta tests! It is my belief that Kavela will be a winner in the vertical of scaling the consumption of artificial intelligence.

Most of our workflows today are manual, in Claude/Codex CLIs. Every workflow that works deserves a harness that can consume the intricacies, rulebooks and guidance it requires to succeed reliably, every single time.

Kavela is that: a platform to scale prompts into repeatable workflows, with observability, task management and connectors all in one.

Agents on Kavela are long-running and optimised for dynamic use. They maintain persistent file context, so Git repos run. Each agent run spins up an isolated computer to run tasks, so no two agents compete for the same resources, while still sharing and syncing files dynamically.

Claude/Codex subs are one click away from being used on the platform.

Kavela MCP allows you to promote sessions in your local workspace into repeatable cloud automations with a single ask.

As mentioned, the closed beta is now live, and I am looking for testers! If creating reliable agent-first automations has been a pain for you, or you are looking to scale your use of tokens by bringing your workflows into the cloud, I want to work with you.

Quick Links: App: https://kavela.ai Docs: https://docs.kavela.ai Closed Beta GC: https://t.me/kavelaAI

story_text.value:
Hey HN,

Loudwalk (https://loudwalk.com/?from=hn) is an app I built for myself to review my Anki flashcards out loud on a walk, and am excited to share today.

Anki has changed my life and is probably the best habit I've managed to stick with. Apart from helping at my tech day-job and remembering random things I find interesting (relatives' birthdays, quotes, poetry), it allowed me to become conversational in Russian in 2 years and complete the first year of a French university degree in Art History - all while working full-time as CTO and co-founder at my company. I have an average memory at best, and it is crazy what Anki unlocks with consistency.

Recently I've been exploring how interacting with LLMs by voice can help me spend less time at a screen and more time active and outdoors, for two main reasons:

- wanting to be more active/healthy as I'm in my mid-thirties and starting to get back pain

- just had a newborn and spend a lot of time carrying him or doing chores around the house

Most of my time sitting at my desk is spent waiting for coding agents and reviewing Anki cards. After building Notiferry (https://notiferry.com/) to forward macOS notifications to my iPhone, the next obvious move was Loudwalk: an LLM asks your card questions, listens to your spoken answer, and grades it. Voice reviews give a cadence I don't have on screen, cutting my daily review time in half (from 90 minutes to 45), and walking while reviewing helps both memorization and mood. Time simply doesn't have the same flavor staring at a monitor vs walking in nature or holding your baby.

What Loudwalk does:

- Import your decks with full history and media from Anki (and export back to Anki with no lock-in; includes a starter deck and CSV import if you don't use Anki yet)

- Start a voice review from any deck (works with Siri so your phone stays in your pocket)

- Spoken grading + "deep dives": if you stumble on a card or want context, ask out loud to start a live conversation on the subject, with live web fact-checking when dates or connections matter. Say "next" to return to your queue

- Question rewording: rephrases questions so you memorize the concept, not the exact card wording

- Phonetic grading + deterministic timing: on-device STT mangles proper nouns, so the LLM grades phonetically/semantically against your card's answer, while response-time caps (Again/Hard/Good/Easy) are applied deterministically in code

- On-device speech recognition; grading and deep dives use OpenAI models (a mix of GPT-6 Luna and Sol + GPT-Live-1)

It runs on iPhone (iOS 26) and Apple silicon Mac (macOS 26). No Android or Windows.

I haven't planned to open-source it for now as I'm seeing if it can support me working on it long-term. Visual reviews (Anki-style) are free forever; voice reviews require a subscription ($9.99/mo) after a 7-day trial (no account or credit card required). Sync across Mac and iPhone uses append-only JSONL review logs in your own iCloud Drive - no server in the sync path, and visual reviews + sync + export work offline forever.

I switched to Loudwalk over 3 months ago (>3k spoken reviews) with first-class support for English and French, plus a CLI so coding agents can add cards at the end of a study session.

Happy to answer any questions about the app or spaced repetition!

title.value: Show HN: Loudwalk – Review your Anki deck out loud on a walk

story_text.value:
Hey Everyone, After getting frustrated by Claude rewriting key functions and still making the test pass, was tinkering around with a review tool, that would track the assumptions and decisions the agent took, without me digging through the entire session. So ended up building Sonah. Sonah is basically a code reviewer that not only reads the code and diff but also the agent session that wrote the code, to understand the assumptions, and decisions your agent took along the way. And highlight important parts of the code that need your attention.

Sonah uses your existing claude code/codex subscription (claude preferred for higher context window). You can try using below: npm install -g getsonah sonah doctor cd your-project && sonah review --format html --output ~/review.html

story_text.value:
About two years ago, I built KeyboardStack as my first macOS app. Since then, I've kept working on it, fixing bugs, improving performance, and adding new features.

I spend most of my day in front of a computer, and one thing that always bothered me was constantly switching between my keyboard and mouse or trackpad, even for something as simple as clicking a button.

I wanted to make my entire Mac keyboard-first, not just my browser or terminal.

So I built KeyboardStack, a native macOS app that lets you navigate, click, and scroll using just your keyboard.

There are already some great tools like Shortcat, Vimac, and Mouseless. My goal was to combine the best of both approaches:

Hint Mode: Displays keyboard hints over clickable elements like buttons and links. Type a few letters to interact with them.

Grid Mode: Displays a grid over your screen. Type a few letters to click anywhere, even when an element isn't detected as clickable.

There are also modes for scrolling, moving the cursor, and navigating windows in Mission Control.

You can learn more at https://keyboardstack.com

I'm still actively working on KeyboardStack and would love to hear your feedback, especially from people who already use tools like Shortcat, Homerow, or Mouseless.

title.value: Show HN: Shortcat meets Mouseless, keyboard-first way to control your Mac

story_text.value:
With Bun-Bun, we are trying to solve two distinct problems.

1. The saved lists everywhere - the food recommendations usually live inside WhatsApp chats, saved Instagram reels, bookmarks, and to-do notes. None of them have the capability to remind you when you are near something that you always wished to try. Bun-bun is capable of assigning a geolocation tag to your saved list by identifying the restaurant name and the dish name that you wanted to try, and remind you when you are near that specific restaurant.

2. The opinions expressed as star ratings - strangers on the internet, in Google Reviews, and everywhere else have opinions. Food is a very personal thing, and you might not always like what has 4.9 stars with 50,000 reviews on Google. So we build a trusted circle of similar-taste-buddies, where all the food that you and your buddies have liked is listed in a single list arranged by distance.

App is now available on App store and Play store

title.value: Show HN: BunBun – A location aware food companion

story_text.value:
Hi HN, I'm Simon. I built Basteon because I wanted one place to see all my money (bank accounts, brokers, cash, gold, real estate, crypto) without giving a company a copy of my transactions/net-worth.

video walkthrough, about 3 minutes: https://x.com/novospes/status/2110710334818222539

How it works:

Your data lives in an encrypted sqlite database on your phone. There is no account with a stored copy of your transactions on our side.

We have a dumb (no storing/logging) sync-server that connects to Enable Banking, but the actual authorization tokens to get the bank data lives on your device. This is the UX-friendly way.

But for people who want a trust-less setup. The server itself will be open-sourced

We're planning to relaunch Q4 2026.
